questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state how political culture is established empirically
questions.stem: Political culture is described as the distribution of political attitudes across a population. How is that distribution established in practice?

options.text: By surveying a sample of citizens and asking each the same questions
By reading the statutes a country has enacted over the past century
options.misconception: treats written law as a record of what citizens believe

options.text: By counting how many parties are able to contest a national election
options.misconception: reads the party system as a measurement of popular attitudes

options.text: By measuring the average income earned by citizens each year
options.misconception: substitutes material conditions for political beliefs

questions.explanation: Political culture is measured by putting the same questions to a sample of citizens and reporting how the answers are distributed, including how they differ between groups. That is what makes it a distribution of attitudes rather than an impression. Statutes record what a country has decided to do, the number of parties records how the electoral system is structured, and income records material conditions; none of the three tells a researcher what people think about politics. So the survey with a common instrument is what establishes the distribution.
questions.hint: Ask what instrument would make answers from different citizens comparable.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a participant culture from an observer culture
questions.stem: One political culture is called a participant culture and another an observer culture. What is the difference between them?

options.text: In one people engage in politics directly; in the other they mostly watch it
In one voting is voluntary; in the other it is compulsory every time
options.misconception: fixes the distinction on whether the state compels participation

options.text: In one parties are numerous; in the other two parties always dominate
options.misconception: reads the distinction as one about party-system type

options.text: In one the press is free; in the other the press is state controlled
options.misconception: treats press freedom as the defining cultural difference

questions.explanation: The distinction concerns how people relate to politics: whether they join organisations, campaign, petition, demonstrate and discuss, or whether they remain spectators who follow events and vote when asked. Whether the state compels a vote, how many parties exist, and how free the press is are all features of institutions that may be found alongside either culture. The term was coined to describe a style of political engagement, not to sort countries by their electoral rules or by their media regime, so none of those belongs in the definition.
questions.hint: Ask whether people act on politics or only follow it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a political value from a political attitude
questions.stem: A researcher separates a political value from a political attitude. What exactly is the difference between the two?

options.text: A value is an enduring commitment; an attitude is a position on one question
A value is what people say; an attitude is what they do at elections
options.misconception: turns a difference in kind into a difference between words and deeds

options.text: A value is held by one social group; an attitude by the whole population
options.misconception: assigns each concept to a different population instead of a different level

options.text: A value is found by survey; an attitude by watching how people vote
options.misconception: treats the two methods as two different definitions

questions.explanation: A value is a general and durable commitment about what ought to be, while an attitude is the position a person takes on one specified question. The two can move independently, so a person may hold a firm value and still oppose a particular measure aimed at it, or support a measure for reasons that carry no commitment of the relevant kind at all. The gap between what people say and how they vote is a concern about how well an attitude is measured rather than the definition of the two concepts, and either can be measured in more than one way.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two is general and which attaches to one question.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state what the account of political socialisation singles out
questions.stem: Political socialisation is defined as the process through which people acquire their political views. What does that definition single out?

options.text: That political views are learned, mainly early, from a few recurring sources
That political views are inherited unchanged from a person's own parents
options.misconception: reads socialisation as literal inheritance with no later revision

options.text: That political views are chosen freely once a person reaches adulthood
options.misconception: removes the learning element that the word socialisation names

options.text: That political views are imposed by whichever government holds power
options.misconception: mistakes a source of political influence for the learning process

questions.explanation: The word socialisation names a learning process, and the standard account places the family first, then school and peers, with media and workplace added later. It does not claim that learning equals unchanged inheritance, since people revise their views across a lifetime, and it does not claim that views are chosen in a vacuum, since the choices are made inside what has already been learned. Nor does the term say anything about which government is in power: a state can push an official view, but the process it is exploiting is the one the definition names.
questions.hint: Ask what the word socialisation itself asserts about how views are acquired.

options.misconception: assigns each agent a subject matter rather than a reach

questions.explanation: The three agents differ in reach, timing and content. The family is earliest and most intimate, but it is uneven, because it can only socialise the children in a household and what it transmits depends on that household. The school reaches nearly every child on a shared curriculum, which is why it is the agent able to impose a common national narrative. Peers matter most in adolescence and early adulthood, when views are tested against people outside the home. So reach rises from family to school while the timing of peak influence shifts the other way.
questions.hint: Ask which agent can reach almost every child on the same material.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain the media's role as a source of political learning
questions.stem: Mass media is treated as an agent of political socialisation. What does that treatment rest on?

options.text: On the media selecting, framing and repeating a limited range of events
On the media reporting every event with no element of selection at all
options.misconception: assumes coverage is complete and unfiltered by editorial choice

options.text: On the media being read only by people with no other political source
options.misconception: treats the media as the sole channel of political learning

options.text: On the media holding the legal power to decide what a legislature considers
options.misconception: confuses agenda influence with a formal right to set it

questions.explanation: What the media pass on is not the political world but a version of it, and the version is produced by three operations: choosing which events to cover, describing them in frames that make sense of them, and repeating some of them often enough to raise their salience. Those operations are enough for the media to shape what people think about, without any legal authority. A complete and unfiltered record is not something any medium produces, most people draw on several sources, and the power to decide what a legislature considers belongs to the legislature's own rules. So the influence is a matter of selection, not of authority.
questions.hint: Ask what stands between the events and what a reader learns about them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: relate a political system to the regime that operates within it
questions.stem: A political system is a set of stable rules; a regime is the way authority is actually obtained and used. Which claim relates the two correctly?

options.text: A regime is the practice within a system's rules, democratic or otherwise
A regime is the written constitution and a system is everything else
options.misconception: reduces the regime to a document rather than to practice

options.text: A regime and a system are simply two names for one identical thing
options.misconception: denies the gap that the distinction exists to capture

options.text: A regime can exist without any rules governing how it operates
options.misconception: allows a pattern of authority to stand apart from any rules

questions.explanation: The system supplies the standing rules: how offices are filled, which powers exist and how decisions are made. The regime describes the practice within them, including whether those offices are genuinely competed for and whether the rules are respected. That gap is precisely why one constitutional text can be lived through by a democracy and by an authoritarian regime, and why regime analysis looks at conduct rather than at the document. A regime is not the constitution itself, not a synonym for the system, and it cannot be described as a practice that no rule governs at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rules are what is written or what actually happens.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state the three features that define authoritarian rule
questions.stem: Authoritarian rule is conventionally defined by three features appearing together. Which set of three fits that definition?

options.text: Concentrated power, restricted pluralism, and weak accountability
A written constitution, competitive elections, and a professional service
options.misconception: assembles features that belong to democratic systems into one definition

options.text: A single legislative party, frequent referendums, and a large cabinet
options.misconception: mixes a party-state feature with instruments of direct democracy

options.text: Free speech, an independent judiciary, and a regular civil service
options.misconception: lists the checks whose absence defines authoritarianism instead

questions.explanation: The definition works on three dimensions at once. Power is concentrated at the top rather than dispersed among institutions that can check one another. Political pluralism is restricted, so organised opposition is unable to threaten the government's position. And accountability is weak, because the executive is not answerable to a body able to remove it. The other three sets either list the checks whose absence makes a regime authoritarian, or combine a feature of a one-party state with instruments of direct democracy; no definition requires a constitution, competitive elections or free speech.
questions.hint: Ask which three things an authoritarian regime has instead of the checks a democracy has.

questions.learningObjective: identify the element that distinguishes a totalitarian regime
questions.stem: One one-party state holds no elections and permits no opposition. A second does the same, but also insists that its members accept one account of society and enforces it in schools and the arts. What sets the second apart?

options.text: An official ideology it requires people to hold, which is the totalitarian element
The absence of elections, which it shares with the first one-party state
options.misconception: credits a feature the two states hold in common with the difference

options.text: The banning of opposition parties, which both of the states have done
options.misconception: credits a common restriction with separating the two cases

options.text: A single leader chosen without a contest, as in the first state
options.misconception: treats uncontested succession as the distinguishing feature

questions.explanation: Totalitarianism is separated from other authoritarian regimes by ideology. It claims a complete account of how society works and then tries to bring the population into agreement with it, reaching into the family, the school and cultural life, where ordinary authoritarian rule usually leaves some space alone. The two features the first state also has — no elections and no permitted opposition — are shared with every authoritarian regime and so cannot be what distinguishes the second. What is new is the demand that a belief be held, not merely that a party be obeyed. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two states is trying to change what people believe, not just whom they obey.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why hybrid regimes are hard to score
questions.stem: A regime holds competitive elections that opposition parties can win, yet the winner then uses office to restrict the opposition's ability to compete next time. How should such a regime be scored, and why is it awkward?

options.text: Between democracy and authoritarianism, because its features point both ways
As fully democratic, because the presence of elections settles the question
options.misconception: lets one democratic criterion settle a case the others contradict

options.text: As fully authoritarian, because the incumbent's conduct overrides the result
options.misconception: lets one authoritarian criterion override the others by fiat

options.text: As a monarchy, because limiting rivals resembles hereditary succession
options.misconception: maps an electoral tactic onto a form of succession

questions.explanation: Scoring is awkward precisely because the features conflict. Meaningful competition is one of the criteria for a democracy, and an incumbent's use of office to foreclose the next contest is one of the criteria for authoritarianism. A composite measure scores both, so the case lands between the two categories, and the intermediate position rather than any single detail is what makes the classification hard to defend. Choosing the democratic criterion on its own, or the authoritarian one on its own, is not a measurement but a decision, and neither resembles a hereditary arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask which criteria point towards democracy and which point the other way.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify a democratic deficit
questions.stem: A country holds regular competitive elections and a legislature that can dismiss its governments, yet the legislature is routinely bypassed on an important class of decisions handed to an unelected body. What is at work?

options.text: A democratic deficit, since the institutions exist without real control
A procedural democracy, since elections and dismissal are both available
options.misconception: accepts the procedural test as if it settled the question of control

options.text: A majoritarian bias, since unelected bodies usually favour the largest party
options.misconception: invents a party bias that the scenario never mentions

options.text: An electoral threshold, since a second body is effectively a second poll
options.misconception: equates a decision-making body with an election

questions.explanation: A democratic deficit exists where the formal architecture is present but the decisive power is not accountable through it. A procedural reading is satisfied by competitive elections and by the ability of a legislature to dismiss a government, and precisely because such cases pass that test there is a need for a second term to name what the test misses. Neither the district-size rule that produces a seat bonus nor a vote threshold bears on the existence of an unelected body taking decisions; both are features of how a chamber is composed.
questions.hint: Ask where the decisive decisions are made and who can be punished for them.

questions.learningObjective: match procedural and substantive definitions of democracy

questions.learningObjective: identify what the four dimensions of democracy measure
questions.stem: An assessment scores a state on free and fair competition, broad participation, freedom of expression, and a rule of law that binds public officials. What is that assessment measuring?

options.text: The dimensions along which a regime can be called democratic or not
The institutions a democracy must own, counted as physical buildings
options.misconception: turns scored properties into a list of buildings required

options.text: The stages a country must pass through on the road to democracy
options.misconception: reads a set of simultaneous properties as a sequence

options.text: The number of parties needed before a democracy can be called one
options.misconception: confuses the dimensions of democracy with party-system type

questions.explanation: Competition, participation, liberty of expression and the rule of law are the dimensions along which a regime is assessed, and the value of assessing them together is that a state can pass on one and fail on another. They are properties to be scored, not buildings a country must own, not stages it travels through in order, and not a condition about how many parties exist.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reading a regime from its features
questions.learningObjective: classify a regime from mutually reinforcing features
questions.stem: An observer reports that a state has a legislature, elections that regularly change which party governs, and courts able to strike down executive acts. On those features alone, what classification is supported?

options.text: A competitive democracy, since each feature checks the others in turn
An electoral autocracy, since the presence of elections settles nothing more
options.misconception: dismisses a reported feature without any reason given

options.text: A hybrid regime, since having courts rules out full democratic standing
options.misconception: treats one check as evidence against democratic standing

options.text: A one-party state, since frequent alternation shows tight party discipline
options.misconception: reads a change of governing party as evidence of one-party control

questions.explanation: These features are mutually reinforcing, and that is the reason for assessing them together. Elections that can turn a government out constrain the executive at the moment people judge it, and courts that can invalidate executive acts supply a check that does not depend on waiting for the next election, so a government that has lost a vote still faces the law. A report of this kind therefore supports a competitive classification, and neither a set of courts nor a change of governing party provides any support for the hybrid or one-party readings offered against it.
questions.hint: Ask what each reported feature would be worth if the other two were absent.

questions.learningObjective: test a democratic claim against a reported institutional gap
questions.stem: A state claims full democratic standing because all parties contest fair elections. Its own report also records that the courts cannot review the legality of executive acts. What tells against the claim?

options.misconception: reads a feature consistent with the claim as evidence against it

questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages through which a policy passes
questions.stem: A policy is eventually reviewed and, on the basis of that review, amended. Put these four stages in the order a policy passes through them, from the first to the last.

options.text: The problem is defined and placed on the government's agenda for action
A decision fixes which group is targeted and with what instrument
The chosen instrument is put into practice by those who must deliver it
The results are reviewed and the findings are fed back to the agenda

questions.explanation: The sequence is causal rather than conventional. A problem has to be defined and put on the agenda before anyone can be asked to decide anything, because a decision taken on an undefined problem resolves whatever the drafter happened to assume was at issue. The decision then settles the target and the instrument together, and nothing can be delivered before both are fixed. Implementation follows the decision, and review can only come afterwards, since there is nothing to assess until the instrument has actually been used. So the order is A, B, C, D.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why values and attitudes must be separated
questions.stem: Explain why a political value and a political attitude have to be treated as separate things, and give one consequence of collapsing them.

answer.exemplar: A value is a general and durable commitment about what ought to be, such as a belief that equality of opportunity matters more than efficiency in the distribution of chances, while an attitude is the position taken on one specified question, such as whether a particular tax increase should be passed. The two move independently: someone may hold equality as a firm value and still oppose a measure aimed at it because the method is judged wrong, and someone may support the same measure for reasons that carry no equality commitment at all. Collapsing them produces errors in both directions, because it hides a value that is present but qualified and invents one that is absent whenever a single liberal attitude turns up. It also misreads change, since attitudes can move while the underlying value never shifted.

questions.explanation: A model answer must show that the two can move independently, and name a specific error that follows from treating them as one.
questions.hint: Ask whether a value can be held firmly while a particular position on one question is rejected.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why hybrid regimes are hard to score
questions.stem: Explain why a regime combining democratic and authoritarian features is hard to score on a composite measure, and say what such a measure must do about it.

answer.exemplar: A composite score is normally built from separate criteria that point in one direction, with competition, participation and accountability counting towards democracy and the concentration of power, restrictions on opposition and the absence of checks counting towards authoritarianism. A hybrid case scores well on some of the first and on some of the second, so its total depends on how many criteria of each kind the measure happens to contain and how heavily each one is weighted. That is a weakness in the arithmetic rather than a mere dispute about labels, because two measures built from the same number of criteria can place the same country in different categories. The measure therefore has to report the profile as well as the total, and to publish its weights, so that a reader can see whether a middling score reflects a settled regime or the two features arriving together.

questions.explanation: A model answer should identify the conflicting criteria, show that the total depends on the weighting, and say what the measure must report to be readable.
questions.hint: Ask what the score does when some criteria point one way and others point the other way.

questions.learningObjective: identify what a grievance alone does not supply
questions.stem: A movement has a serious grievance and a widely shared sense of injustice, but no organisation, no money and no way to contact its members. What is still missing?

options.text: Resources and an organisation able to turn grievance into sustained action
A larger number of people who share the grievance even more strongly
options.misconception: assumes a bigger pool of aggrieved people solves the problem of organising

options.text: A formal legal status, without which no campaign can be conducted
options.misconception: makes legal standing a precondition for having any organisation at all

options.text: A single leader able to issue instructions to whoever is willing to act

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the two kinds of social capital
questions.stem: Social capital is described as coming in two kinds. How do those two kinds differ?

options.text: One binds together people who are alike; the other connects those who differ
One is formed inside the family; the other is formed inside the workplace
options.misconception: fixes each kind to an institution rather than to a similarity

options.text: One is measured by trust; the other by the number of members enrolled
options.misconception: treats a difference in measurement as the difference between kinds

options.text: One closes a group inward; the other is found only within family networks
options.misconception: confines bridging ties to a single institution

questions.explanation: The two kinds are distinguished by who is joined to whom. Bonding ties people who already share a background, which supports solidarity and the enforcement of norms inside a group but can also insulate it from anyone outside. Bridging ties people from different groups together, and that is what allows trust and information to cross a division. Neither kind belongs to a particular institution, since bonding and bridging both occur in families, workplaces and neighbourhoods, and the difference between them is not in how they are measured but in the similarity of the members. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask what the people in each network have in common.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why political socialisation is not confined to childhood
questions.stem: Why is political socialisation described as a lifelong process rather than something finished in childhood?

options.text: Adults keep revising their views in response to events, work and the media
Children have no capacity to acquire political views of any kind
options.misconception: denies childhood learning in order to defend a lifelong account

options.text: Only people below a certain age can be influenced politically at all
options.misconception: invents an age ceiling on political learning in general

options.text: The childhood agents simply resume working in exactly the same way
options.misconception: assumes the same agents and the same methods carry on unchanged

questions.explanation: The account of socialisation is lifelong because the political world keeps supplying new reasons to revise a view: an election that goes badly, a scandal, a change of government, a new job or a campaign that reaches someone who had paid no attention. This is why an adult's allegiance can shift after decades of stability, and why a party can lose voters it assumed it already had. Children are fully capable of acquiring political views, so the childhood emphasis is about timing and about first impressions that are not yet contested, not about capacity. And the later agents are different ones, operating in different settings, not the childhood agents resumed unchanged. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask what supplies a reason to change one's mind after the age of twenty.

questions.learningObjective: state what a policy's target decision settles
questions.stem: Choosing which population a policy targets is treated as a design decision. What does that choice actually settle?

options.text: Which group receives the benefit, before any instrument is chosen
Which office will deliver the policy, during the implementation stage
options.misconception: moves a design decision into the stage that follows adoption

options.text: Which party will oppose the measure, once the measure has been adopted
options.misconception: treats opposition as something a government sets as a matter of design

options.text: Which minister sponsors the proposal, at the very start of the process
options.misconception: substitutes political sponsorship for the question of who benefits

questions.explanation: Targeting comes early in the design sequence, because the target determines who gains and who pays, and the instrument is then chosen as the means of reaching that group. Choosing the instrument first is a recognised failure, because a rule or a subsidy picked without a target in mind can end up reaching a different group altogether, and the distributional claim made for the policy will then be wrong. Delivery arrangements, opposition and sponsorship are all real considerations, but none of them is what the target decision settles. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two design choices has to come first for the other to make sense.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an output from an outcome
questions.stem: A housing programme reports that it has built the number of units it planned, and that rents in its target city have continued to rise faster than wages. Which reading of the two results is sound?

options.text: They do not contradict each other, since building units need not lower rents
They contradict each other, so one of the two published figures is false
options.misconception: treats divergence between two measures as a logical contradiction

options.text: Rising rents show the programme failed, whatever it managed to build
options.misconception: lets one indicator settle a question about a different outcome

options.text: Rising rents show the programme worked, since demand must have risen sharply
options.misconception: reads pressure on prices as evidence of successful delivery

questions.explanation: An output and an outcome are different measures of the same policy, and a programme can meet its output target while missing the effect it was built to produce. Building a set number of units says nothing on its own about the price of housing, which depends on how many dwellings exist in total, where they are, whether the people who need them can reach them, and what is being built beside them. Two figures pointing in different directions are not a contradiction, and neither can be treated as decisive on its own. Demand for housing rising is a statement about pressure on prices, not a measure of what a programme achieved. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask what the number of units is a measure of, and what rent is a measure of.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the direction in which feedback runs
questions.stem: A new benefit is means-tested, must be claimed by visiting offices that are known for long waits, and now reaches a small share of those entitled to it. Which description of the feedback is right?

options.text: A reinforcing loop, since the burden of claiming discourages claiming
A self-correcting loop, since fewer claims mean shorter waits for the rest
options.misconception: treats the cost borne by applicants as a cost that corrects itself

options.text: No effect at all, since the burden falls on administrators, not applicants
options.misconception: assigns the cost of a means test to the wrong side of the counter

options.text: A reversing effect, since low take-up will soon make voters abolish it
options.misconception: jumps from a low figure to a decision that has not been taken

questions.explanation: Feedback runs in a direction, and here the costs the policy imposes feed straight back into the behaviour it was meant to change. A means test that requires repeated visits, delivered through offices known for long queues, raises the cost of claiming; fewer eligible people claim; the programme is then judged to have failed to reach the people it was designed for; and that judgement supplies an argument for cutting it. That is a reinforcing loop, not a self-correcting one, since the burden falls on applicants rather than on administrators, and nothing in the description has yet produced any decision to abolish the scheme. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask who pays the cost, and what they do about it next time.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: test an announced outcome against the delivery mechanism
questions.stem: A ministry announces that records will be linked so that a person's file follows them between regions. The regions run incompatible systems and cannot exchange data. What is wrong with the design?

options.text: Nothing in it provides a way to move a record between the systems
The ministry must publish the project's cost before any work can start
options.misconception: treats a transparency requirement as a barrier to delivery

options.text: The regions will each have to appoint a named person responsible
options.misconception: treats naming an owner as though it prevented the technical obstacle

options.text: The work will take longer than a single electoral term to complete
options.misconception: raises a risk to the project's continuation as a barrier to its start

questions.explanation: A promised outcome needs a mechanism that actually connects the parties involved, and a promise to link records needs a way to move a record. Where the systems are incompatible, nothing in the description supplies one, so the announcement has stated a wish rather than a delivery plan, and goodwill between offices will not produce an interoperability that has not been built. Publishing a cost, appointing a responsible officer and finishing within one term are all sensible, and the first two make a project more accountable, but none of them creates the missing technical link. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask what physical or technical step would move a file, and whether the design contains one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The school as a common agent
questions.learningObjective: explain the school's distinctive reach as a socialising agent
questions.stem: A ministry changes the history curriculum so that every school teaches one agreed national account of how the country formed. Why is the school a powerful agent here?

options.text: It is present for nearly every child and delivers the same material to all
It is the only agent that reaches children before the family does
options.misconception: reverses the order in which the family and the school act

options.text: It is the only agent whose influence lasts unchanged into adult life
options.misconception: credits the classroom with a permanence the later agents lack

options.text: It is the only agent able to reward a child for repeating what it teaches
options.misconception: invents an incentive that schooling does not use to secure belief

questions.explanation: The school's power is coverage combined with uniformity. Almost every child is enrolled and receives the same material over the same years, so a single curriculum change reaches a whole generation with one version of the past, which is precisely how a common national narrative is produced. The family comes first in time rather than the school, and the agents that shape adult views are media, work and political events rather than the classroom. Schools reward performance in examinations rather than assent to a claim, so the incentive in the last option is not theirs to give. So the answer is A.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Matching an instrument to a problem
questions.learningObjective: match a policy instrument to the problem it addresses
questions.stem: A city wants less traffic in its centre. The benefit of clearing traffic falls on the whole city, while the cost of driving less falls on the driver alone, so nothing happens. Which instrument addresses that?

options.text: A charge on entry, which changes the price of the action causing harm
A leaflet to every household, which tells residents what the traffic costs
options.misconception: presumes a lack of knowledge where the problem is the incentive

options.text: A new office to coordinate traffic, which organises those already willing
options.misconception: applies a structural fix to a problem of individual incentive

options.text: A committee of drivers to advise the council, which gives them a voice
options.misconception: supplies a say to a group whose obstacle is the cost of acting

questions.explanation: A problem of this shape is one of collective action, and it is met with an instrument that changes prices, because a charge makes the individual cost of driving fall on the driver who causes the congestion and internalises a benefit that is otherwise spread across the whole city. Information does not help where the incentive rather than the knowledge is the obstacle, since a resident can already see what congestion costs. Restructuring who decides matters where the difficulty is coordination among willing actors, and giving drivers a voice addresses none of these, because the obstacle here is that no single driver has reason to act first. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask whether the obstacle is knowing what to do, or having a reason to do it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute a net distributional effect across groups
questions.stem: A table reports two rows. Three million residents each gain 40 units, and two million residents each lose 25 units. What is the net effect across the population?

options.text: A net gain of 70 million, since 120 million is gained and 50 million lost
A net loss of 50 million, since only the losing row should be counted
options.misconception: reports the loss side and omits the gain from the same calculation

options.text: A net gain of 15 per person, since 40 minus 25 equals exactly 15
options.misconception: subtracts per-person amounts drawn from groups of different sizes

options.text: No net effect, since the two rows hold different numbers of people
options.misconception: refuses to net two figures merely because the groups differ in size

questions.explanation: A net effect is found by multiplying each group's size by its per-person amount, then netting the two results against each other. Three million times forty is a gain of 120 million, and two million times twenty-five is a loss of 50 million, leaving a net gain of 70 million for the population as a whole. Subtracting forty from twenty-five per person mixes groups of different sizes and different amounts, and two figures can be netted against one another however different the groups are. What a net figure cannot show is how that total is shared inside the larger group, so nothing follows from it about the typical person's position. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Multiply each row first, and only then subtract.

questions.learningObjective: read co-movement in trust evidence
questions.stem: A survey reports that trust in the courts has stayed flat, trust in the body that allocates public money has fallen sharply, and reported fraud by that body has risen over the same period. What is safest?

options.text: The two series move together, which is consistent but not shown to be causal
Fraud caused the fall in trust, because the timing settles the direction
options.misconception: reads co-movement as proof of one particular causal direction

options.text: Falling trust caused the fraud, since distrust is known to produce it
options.misconception: asserts the reverse causal direction on the same evidence

options.text: The two are unrelated, since trust cannot respond to news at all
options.misconception: denies a responsiveness the flat series for the courts does not show

questions.explanation: Two series moving together is an association, and the reading it supports is that where people believe money is being misused, their trust in the body handling it falls. It does not establish the direction, since rising fraud might damage trust, falling trust might make fraud easier, and the two could sustain each other; a comparison over time cannot separate these. Simultaneity is not proof of causation in either direction, and the last option is contradicted by the body named in the report having moved at all. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask what two series changing together does and does not establish about direction.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the three tests of revolution to a case
questions.stem: A government is overthrown, the constitution is suspended, and the incoming ruler abolishes the previous legislature and the parties that filled it. Which tests are met, and what is open?

options.text: Two are met, on the source of authority and on the form of regime
All three are met, since the wider political order has also been overturned
options.misconception: counts a change of regime as proof of a change of the wider order

options.text: Only one is met, namely the change in the source of sovereign authority
options.misconception: ignores the regime change that abolishing a legislature represents

options.text: None is met, since one incoming ruler made every one of the changes
options.misconception: makes the identity of the change-maker decide what kind of change it was

questions.explanation: The three tests ask separately whether the source of sovereign authority was replaced, whether the form of regime changed, and whether the wider political order was overturned. An overthrow that installs a ruler with the power to do the rest answers the first, and suspending a constitution while abolishing the legislature and its parties answers the second, because those were the institutions that constituted the old regime. What remains open is the third, and a description of events at the top does not by itself establish a transformation of the whole political order. The identity of the person who made the changes has no bearing on which tests are met. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask separately about authority, about regime, and about the wider order.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What is at stake in reform and revolution
questions.learningObjective: identify what separates a reform from a revolutionary claim
questions.stem: One movement has won a change to the eligibility rule for a single service through petition and legislation. Another seeks to replace the state that governs its members and is prepared to take up arms. What is the difference that matters?

options.text: Whether authority over the political order is at stake, not the intensity felt
Whether legal means were used, since a lawful change is not a revolution
options.misconception: makes the choice of method the definition rather than the aim

options.text: Whether a majority of the population backs it, since numbers settle the matter
options.misconception: lets size of support stand in for the object of the demand

options.text: Whether a single leader is named, since movements now need a figurehead
options.misconception: makes personal leadership the dividing line between the two cases

questions.explanation: What separates the two is what each is claiming. The first confines its demand to the content of a rule inside institutions that remain in place, which is why petition and legislation are the right means and why a victory leaves the source of authority untouched. The second makes authority itself the object of the claim, and the willingness to take up arms follows from that aim rather than defining it. A revolutionary movement may be entirely law-abiding for years, and a reform movement may lack a majority, a leader or a constituency, none of which is the difference the description turns on. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask what each movement wants changed, before asking how it proceeds.

questions.learningObjective: sequence a policy from problem definition to delivery
questions.stem: A problem has been recognised and a government is trying to act on it. Put these four steps in the order the process requires, from the first to the last.

A window opens in the surrounding conditions and a proposal matches it
An entrepreneur secures the agreement of those who are able to decide
The instrument is delivered and the results are fed back to the agenda

questions.explanation: The order is causal, and each step sets up the one after it. A problem has to be defined before anyone can propose a remedy, because an entrepreneur needs something concrete to attach to rather than a grievance. A window then has to open in the surrounding conditions, since a proposal presented outside one has nothing to attach to and remains simply a proposal. The entrepreneur's work follows, converting favourable conditions into an actual decision by securing agreement from those who can take it. Delivery comes last, and only the results of delivery can then be fed back into the agenda. So the order is A, B, C, D.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a distributional conflict
questions.stem: A measure that will cost one group and benefit another is about to be considered. Put these four steps in the order such a conflict normally runs, from the first to the last.

options.text: The distributional effect is estimated before the measure is adopted
The measure is adopted and the affected groups organise in response
Those who lose mount a legal challenge or a campaign against it
Government negotiates a change, or lets the measure lapse

questions.explanation: A distributional conflict runs in a fixed order, and each stage depends on the one before. The effect is estimated before adoption, because an estimate produced afterwards describes a decision already taken and cannot inform it. Mobilisation follows the law rather than preceding it, since a group has nothing concrete to organise against until the measure is in force, which is why a provision that looked painless on paper can generate a campaign afterwards. The challenge or campaign is a distinct stage from the organisation that makes it possible, and only once opposition is actually visible does the government have grounds to negotiate an adjustment or to abandon the measure. So the order is A, B, C, D.
questions.hint: Ask what a group has to organise against before the measure is in force.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: select the features belonging to a substantive definition
questions.stem: A substantive definition of democracy holds that a system must deliver certain things. Which features belong to that definition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Freedom from domination, so that people are not subject to arbitrary power
Equality of opportunity, so that positions are open on comparable terms
Freedom from interference in belief, speech and lawful association
A majority requirement on the outcome of any election that is held
options.misconception: assigns a counting rule to a definition about what a system delivers

options.text: An obligation on every citizen to take part in politics each year
options.misconception: makes compulsory participation one of a democracy's deliverables

questions.explanation: The substantive definition evaluates what the system actually secures for the people in it rather than how offices are filled, and its central demands are freedom from arbitrary power, equality of opportunity, and freedom of conscience, expression and association. These are the things a democracy is said to deliver, not the procedures by which it decides things. A majority rule on an election result sits on the procedural side, because it describes how a decision is taken rather than what that decision delivers, and an obligation to take part in politics is not a demand any account of substantive democracy makes. So the answer is A, B and C.
questions.hint: Ask whether each item is a thing a system delivers or a rule it uses to decide.
